items.title: Wet Belts: The Problems, the Prices and the Cars Worth Considering
items.summary: As manufacturers faced increasingly demanding emissions targets, even tiny improvements in engine efficiency became valuable. Compact three-cylinder engines spread from city cars into family hatchbacks, SUVs and even commercial vehicles, helped by turbocharging and increasingly sophisticated engineering. One of the technologies adopted to reduce friction and mechanical noise was the wet timing…
items.content_html:
Ford's 1.0-litre EcoBoost was an impressive piece of engineering when it arrived in 2012. Despite having just three cylinders and a tiny displacement, it offered lively performance, with outputs eventually reaching 138bhp in the Fiesta.

Official economy figures could approach 65mpg, although achieving anything close to this in everyday driving proved difficult. This wasn't a wet-belt problem, but rather a familiar characteristic of small turbocharged petrol engines, which became increasingly common across Europe.

Unfortunately, the EcoBoost's reputation would eventually become dominated by its oil-immersed timing belt. Designed to reduce friction and mechanical noise, the belt could deteriorate over time, particularly when exposed to degraded or unsuitable engine oil. Fragments of rubber could then accumulate around the oil-pump pickup, restricting lubrication and potentially causing serious engine damage.

For some owners, the consequences were expensive, with failures resulting in damaged turbochargers or even complete engine replacements. The problem became sufficiently well known that the once-celebrated EcoBoost developed an unfortunate reputation among used-car buyers.

Less obviously, the later Fiesta's naturally aspirated 1.1-litre Ti-VCT petrol also used a wet timing belt, meaning avoiding the turbocharged EcoBoost didn't necessarily mean avoiding the technology.


The 1.0 EcoBoost wasn't confined to the Fiesta. Ford fitted it to considerably larger models, including the Focus, Mondeo, C-Max and B-Max, alongside the EcoSport SUV and Transit Courier. That gave buyers the economy and relatively low emissions of a small petrol engine without necessarily sacrificing the practicality of a family car.

Fortunately, preventative wet-belt replacement isn't always as expensive as its reputation suggests. We've found independent garages across Britain advertising replacements for around £600, with some quoting even lower starting prices. Comprehensive packages can include both belts, fresh oil and filter, and oil-system cleaning. Owners should confirm exactly what's included before accepting a quote.

The EcoBoost's reputation has also created an interesting opportunity in the used-car market. We've found several 2013 Fiesta 1.0 EcoBoost examples with around 100,000 miles advertised for approximately £2,000, including the desirable 125PS version. That's a tempting price for a car with excellent road manners, a 0–62mph time of just 9.4 seconds and the potential to approach 50mpg with careful driving.

Many pre-April 2017 EcoBoost Fiestas also qualify for annual road tax of just £20. For buyers prepared to check the service history and budget for preventative maintenance, a well-kept example could represent considerably better value than its reputation might suggest.

But it wasn't the 1.0 EcoBoost where Ford's wet-belt story began. Back in 2007, Ford and Dayco introduced the world's first production automotive belt-in-oil system on the 1.8-litre TDCi diesel, replacing the chain previously used to drive its fuel-injection pump.

The engine appeared in the Focus, C-Max, Mondeo, S-Max and Galaxy, offering a useful middle ground between Ford's smaller 1.6 and more powerful 2.0-litre diesels. Often overlooked, the 125bhp Mondeo 1.8 TDCi offered respectable performance and real-world economy approaching 45–50mpg.

Unlike the later EcoBoost, the 1.8 retained a conventional dry camshaft timing belt, with its oil-immersed belt driving the injection pump instead.

Ford has since moved its revised 1.0 EcoBoost to chain-driven camshafts, including conventional petrol and mild-hybrid applications. Some versions still retain a wet oil-pump belt, however, meaning the transition away from the technology isn't quite as straightforward as it first appears.

Ford's use of wet timing belts didn't end with its smaller petrol engines. In 2016, the company introduced the 2.0-litre EcoBlue diesel, designed for considerably more demanding applications, including the Transit, Transit Custom and, from 2019, the Ranger pickup. The engine also found its way into passenger vehicles, including the Mondeo, Kuga, S-Max and Galaxy.

Unlike the tiny EcoBoost, the EcoBlue was developed with commercial use in mind, where high mileages, heavy loads and long working days are commonplace. Despite these tougher demands, Ford continued using an oil-immersed timing belt, alongside a separate wet belt driving the oil pump.

The consequences of deterioration can be particularly serious for commercial operators, with restricted oil flow potentially causing extensive engine damage and leaving a working vehicle off the road.

Replacement is also a more involved procedure. Access requires substantial dismantling, while the timing cover and sump must be carefully resealed. Some specialists allow a two-day turnaround to give the sealant sufficient curing time, adding to the inconvenience for businesses relying on their vehicles.

While wet-belt problems have become familiar territory for Ford owners, the technology also found its way into less obvious corners of the three-cylinder petrol market, including models from manufacturers with very different reputations for reliability.


Honda is a manufacturer traditionally associated with dependable engineering, and the tenth-generation Civic was no exception in many respects. Introduced in 2017, its entry-level 1.0-litre VTEC Turbo delivered 129PS, respectable performance and impressive fuel economy, making it an appealing alternative to the increasingly common small turbocharged engines from European manufacturers.

However, Honda also adopted an oil-immersed timing belt, introducing a potential weakness into an otherwise accomplished family hatchback. As with Ford's EcoBoost, belt deterioration can lead to restricted oil flow and potentially serious engine damage, making correct servicing and preventative replacement particularly important.

Unlike Ford, Honda fitted this engine to just one generation of the Civic in the UK, with a considerably smaller number of vehicles on the road. Reports of wet-belt failures do exist, but finding widespread owner complaints on the scale associated with Ford or Stellantis is considerably more difficult.

That doesn't necessarily make Honda's design more dependable. With a much smaller population of affected vehicles, there are fewer owners reporting their experiences, making meaningful comparisons difficult.

Honda ultimately discontinued the 1.0 VTEC Turbo when the eleventh-generation Civic arrived in 2022, replacing the petrol range with its e:HEV hybrid powertrain and leaving the wet timing belt behind.


While Honda's use of wet timing belts was limited to a single generation of the Civic, Stellantis took the technology considerably further. Its 1.2-litre PureTech three-cylinder petrol engine appeared across an enormous range of vehicles, initially from Peugeot and Citroën, before spreading to other brands within the expanding Stellantis group, including DS, Vauxhall and Jeep, exposing a wider range of buyers to the same potential problems.

At 1,199cc, the PureTech was also around 20% larger than Ford's 1.0 EcoBoost and many rival three-cylinder petrol engines. This extra capacity gave it an advantage in everyday driving, particularly in heavier vehicles where smaller turbocharged engines could struggle to match their impressive official economy figures. In many applications, the PureTech offered a convincing combination of performance, refinement and real-world fuel economy.

Unfortunately, the engine developed a reputation for premature wet-belt deterioration, with debris potentially restricting oil circulation and causing expensive mechanical damage. However, that doesn't make every PureTech a bad engine or every affected car a poor purchase.

As with the Ford, buyers should pay particular attention to servicing history, correct oil specifications and evidence of belt inspection or replacement. A neglected example could quickly become an expensive mistake, regardless of how attractive its asking price might appear.


As with Ford's EcoBoost, the PureTech's reputation has created some tempting opportunities in the used-car market. A well-maintained example can offer plenty of car for remarkably little money, and the Citroën C4 Cactus is a particularly good example.

We've found 2014–2015 Cactus 1.2 PureTech 110 models with fewer than 100,000 miles advertised for around £2,000. Weighing little more than a tonne, the Citroën offers lively performance, reaching 62mph in approximately 9.3 seconds, while potentially achieving 50mpg in everyday driving.

Maintenance needn't be expensive, either. Garages across the UK advertise wet-belt replacements for under £600, with some starting at £350, including parts, labour, oil and filter. This makes cheaper used examples more appealing, provided buyers check what's included.

The Cactus demonstrates what made the PureTech attractive: a lightweight, practical family car combining performance with economy. With a good service history and appropriate belt maintenance, its damaged reputation could make it a genuine used-car bargain.


Stellantis has, however, been gradually moving away from wet timing belts. Since 2023, the group has introduced a newer generation of its 1.2-litre three-cylinder petrol engine with a timing chain, progressively replacing the older PureTech design across its brands. The 1.2-litre 48V mild-hybrid powertrain has used a timing chain from the outset, combining the petrol engine with electric assistance and an automatic dual-clutch gearbox.

The transition hasn't happened overnight. Some conventional petrol models continued using wet belts alongside newer chain-driven versions, making it important for used-car buyers to check the exact engine rather than relying on registration year alone.

The arrival of STLA Medium-based models, including the latest Peugeot 3008 and Vauxhall Grandland, further illustrates the group's changing direction. Their newer hybrid and electric powertrains leave the original wet-belt PureTech arrangement behind.

After more than a decade of widespread use, wet timing belts are increasingly confined to older Stellantis engine generations and remaining applications. Yet millions of these vehicles will remain on the road for years, and for buyers willing to understand their maintenance requirements, some could still represent excellent value.


Volkswagen is another manufacturer with an interesting connection to wet belts. While the company has previously used oil-immersed belts to drive oil pumps in some of its diesel engines, its newer Ford-developed commercial vehicles have brought wet camshaft timing belts into the range.

The partnership began taking shape in 2020, with the second-generation Amarok arriving in 2023, followed by the latest Transporter in 2025. Both are Ford-based vehicles, with their 2.0-litre diesel models using Ford's EcoBlue engine and its wet timing belt.

For owners facing a wet-belt replacement, however, there's a potentially useful way to reduce the cost. We've found independent Ford specialists advertising comprehensive EcoBlue wet-belt replacements from around £800, approximately £200 less than advertised Volkswagen-specific services. Owners should confirm that the specialist accepts their Volkswagen model and that the quoted work is equivalent.

The Ford connection could also help owners save on other shared mechanical maintenance, rather than automatically turning to Volkswagen specialists for every repair.

It's an unusual arrangement that demonstrates how closely related modern vehicles can be beneath their badges. For existing Transporter and Amarok owners, understanding what's under the bonnet could make an expensive maintenance job considerably more affordable.

Wet timing belts were introduced with good intentions. By running the belt inside engine oil, manufacturers reduced friction, mechanical noise and, crucially, emissions at a time when every gram of CO₂ mattered. Unfortunately, real-world experience showed that the technology could be highly sensitive to servicing standards and oil quality.

Yet that doesn't mean every wet-belt car should be avoided. Millions remain on the road, and many have covered high mileages without issue. For used-car buyers willing to budget for preventative maintenance and verify a strong service history, some wet-belt-equipped cars now represent exceptional value.

Understanding the risks is ultimately more important than fearing the technology itself.

Disclaimer: Prices, specifications and vehicle information are provided for general guidance and may change. Wet-belt applications and maintenance requirements vary by engine and production date. Buyers should verify service histories, confirm manufacturer recommendations and obtain written repair quotations before making decisions. TNY cannot guarantee vehicle reliability or future repair costs.

items.title: TNY Market Watch — Eight Dependable Asian Cars You Can Buy for Under £8,000
items.summary: Buying a dependable used car doesn't have to mean spending a fortune or settling for something dull. With a budget of £8,000, there's an increasingly varied selection of affordable, economical cars available, including models that would have cost considerably more just a few years ago. Asian manufacturers have long enjoyed strong reputations…
items.content_html:
With its sharp styling and spacious interior, the tenth-generation Honda Civic still feels remarkably modern. Its 1.0-litre three-cylinder turbocharged petrol engine produces 126bhp, delivering respectable performance alongside impressive fuel economy.

A budget of £8,000 can secure a 2020 model with around 90,000 miles, while earlier tenth-generation Civics with higher mileages can be found for considerably less. Generous boot space and excellent motorway comfort add to its appeal.

One consideration is the engine's oil-immersed timing belt, which requires careful maintenance and can be expensive to replace. However, well-maintained examples have covered substantial mileages, demonstrating that dependable service is possible when properly looked after. Comprehensive service records and evidence of timing belt maintenance are particularly important.

The original Kia Niro is an excellent choice for families seeking practicality, reliability and economical motoring. Its spacious interior, generous boot and comfortable driving experience make it a particularly appealing all-rounder.

An £8,000 budget offers a good selection of earlier 1.6-litre self-charging hybrids, while higher-mileage plug-in hybrid and fully electric versions are also within reach.

The electric e-Niro is particularly impressive. Its larger 64kWh battery provides up to 282 miles of official WLTP range, making it a remarkably capable used EV at this price point.

The Niro has a strong reputation for dependability, although a comprehensive service history remains important. Higher-mileage electric examples should also have their battery health checked.
The Mazda MX-30 is one of the more unusual affordable electric cars, combining handsome crossover styling with distinctive rear-hinged back doors and a beautifully designed interior. Its 143bhp electric motor delivers smooth performance, while responsive handling makes it surprisingly enjoyable to drive.

An £8,000 budget can secure a 2021 example, often with relatively modest mileage, making it an appealing alternative to more conventional used hatchbacks.

However, its 35.5kWh battery offers just 124 miles of official WLTP range, with considerably less possible in winter. This limits its long-distance appeal, but for shorter commutes and local journeys, particularly with home charging, the MX-30 offers affordable running costs and plenty of character. Battery health and charging functionality are worth checking before purchase.

The MG5 proves that electric motoring doesn't have to be expensive or complicated. It might not be particularly flashy, but this practical estate offers generous passenger space, a large boot and comfortable everyday transport, making it an excellent choice for families or high-mileage drivers.

An £8,000 budget can even stretch to the 61.1kWh Long Range model, offering up to 250 miles of official WLTP range. Its 156bhp electric motor also delivers surprisingly lively performance, while the generous 578-litre boot provides plenty of room for luggage or bulky items.

With relatively simple mechanicals and potentially very low running costs, the MG5 makes a convincing case for affordable electric ownership. Buyers should check battery health, charging functionality and service history before purchasing.

One of the pioneers of modern electric motoring, the Nissan Leaf has become a particularly affordable used family car. The second-generation model brought sharper styling, improved technology and greater practicality, alongside a comfortable interior and generous boot space.

An £8,000 budget can now stretch to the desirable e+ version, featuring a 62kWh battery and up to 239 miles of official WLTP range. Its powerful 217PS electric motor also delivers surprisingly brisk performance.

The Leaf has established a strong reputation for dependability, although battery health remains important when buying. Its CHAdeMO rapid-charging connection is becoming less common, making it particularly appealing to buyers who can charge at home. For the money, it offers an impressive amount of electric family transport.

The Suzuki Swift is proof that small, lightweight cars can still offer enjoyable driving without sacrificing economy or dependability. Its simple mechanicals, compact dimensions and responsive handling make it particularly appealing for everyday motoring.

An £8,000 budget can secure a 2021 mild-hybrid example with around 60,000 miles, offering a modern, economical supermini for relatively little money. Its 1.2-litre four-cylinder petrol engine produces 83bhp, with mild-hybrid assistance helping deliver fuel economy approaching 60mpg.

Weighing well under a tonne, the Swift feels surprisingly lively despite its modest power output. Rear-seat space and boot capacity aren't particularly generous, but low running costs, straightforward maintenance and Suzuki's strong reliability reputation make it an excellent choice for budget-conscious buyers.

With its striking coupé-inspired styling, the first-generation Toyota C-HR remains a distinctive and surprisingly enjoyable family crossover. Its comfortable interior, refined driving experience and strong reliability reputation make it an appealing used purchase.

An £8,000 budget offers plenty of early 1.2-litre turbocharged petrol examples, producing 114bhp from a responsive four-cylinder engine while delivering respectable fuel economy.

However, the real bargain is the exceptionally economical 1.8-litre self-charging hybrid, which is beginning to fall within budget for buyers willing to accept higher mileages. Capable of returning around 55–60mpg in everyday driving, it combines Toyota's proven hybrid technology with the convenience of an automatic transmission.

Rear visibility isn't particularly generous, but the C-HR offers stylish, dependable and economical family transport.

A rear-wheel-drive sports coupé might seem an unusual choice for a dependable, economical used car, but the Toyota GT86 makes a surprisingly convincing case. Its naturally aspirated 2.0-litre boxer engine produces 197bhp, while lightweight construction and beautifully balanced handling make it enormous fun to drive.

An £8,000 budget can secure an early, higher-mileage example, typically from 2012–2013. Despite its sporting character, the GT86 is surprisingly economical, with real-world road tests recording around 38–39mpg in mixed driving.

Reliability is generally reassuring when properly maintained, although buyers should check servicing records, modifications and outstanding recalls. For enthusiasts wanting affordable everyday transport without sacrificing driving enjoyment, the GT86 proves that a genuinely exciting sports car needn't be an impractical or expensive choice.

– From practical family cars to surprisingly affordable electric vehicles and even a genuine sports coupé, our selection demonstrates just how much choice £8,000 can provide in today's used car market.

Some of these models are considerably newer than buyers might expect, while others offer impressive equipment, spacious interiors or exceptionally low running costs. Higher-mileage examples can represent particularly good value, provided they've been maintained properly.

Ultimately, condition and service history matter more than mileage alone. Taking the time to find a well-cared-for example could reward buyers with years of dependable motoring, without the expense of buying something brand new.

All prices, specifications, fuel economy figures and vehicle information were correct to the best of our knowledge at the time of research (October 2026). Used car prices are indicative UK asking prices and will vary depending on condition, mileage, specification and availability.

Fuel economy and electric range figures may differ in real-world driving. Reliability assessments are based on available information and do not guarantee the condition or dependability of individual vehicles. Buyers should carry out appropriate checks before purchasing.

items.title: Paris Motor Show 2026: TNY Explores the Biggest Reveals from Day One
items.summary: The 2026 Paris Motor Show has opened its doors, bringing one of Europe's biggest motoring events back into the spotlight. With more than 100 exhibitors, nearly 60 vehicle manufacturers and dozens of new models and concepts, this year's show promises plenty to explore. Beyond the spectacular concept cars and elaborate displays, Paris…
items.content_html:
We kick off this roundup with the Citroën 2CV, one of the most eagerly anticipated concepts at this year's Paris Motor Show. Measuring just 3.76 metres long, the electric reinterpretation brings the original's distinctive rounded headlights, simple proportions and playful character into the modern era, while promising a practical and spacious interior.

More importantly, Citroën is looking beyond nostalgia. The company is targeting a starting price of around €15,000, with European production planned for 2028. The proposed M1E category could help make such an affordable electric car commercially viable, filling the substantial gap between today's Ami quadricycle and ë-C3 supermini.

For Citroën, this could mark a welcome return to the affordable, unconventional motoring that made the original 2CV famous.


While the return of the 2CV was widely anticipated, Citroën had another surprise waiting in Paris: the electric 2CV Fourgonnette. Inspired by the original 1950s delivery van, the concept combines the revived 2CV's distinctive styling with a practical, boxy rear body designed for carrying goods.

Should it reach production, the Fourgonnette could become a spiritual successor to the much-loved C15 and later Nemo, offering affordable, no-nonsense transport for small businesses. Positioned between the Ami Cargo and ë-C3 Van, with the larger ë-Berlingo above, it could give Citroën four compact electric commercial vehicles, and six electric vans overall when including the ë-Dispatch and ë-Relay.

For now, the Fourgonnette remains a design study, but its combination of character, practicality and potentially low running costs makes a convincing case for production.


DS has unveiled the striking F3VER concept in Paris, previewing a welcome change of direction for its smallest model. Rather than continuing with the crossover formula of today's DS 3, the French premium brand appears ready to return to the traditional hatchback proportions that made the original DS 3 so distinctive.

Measuring 4.19 metres long, the electric concept combines dramatic lighting, sculpted bodywork and a more athletic stance with the promise of greater everyday practicality.

Expected to influence the next-generation DS N°3, the F3VER could represent a much-needed return to the compact, stylish hatchback that first established DS as a standalone premium contender.


TNY Design Studio imagines how the F3VER could evolve into a showroom-ready DS N°3, retaining its distinctive styling with more conventional production details. Expected around 2028, the electric hatchback would sit above the Peugeot e-208 in Stellantis's hierarchy, potentially sharing the forthcoming STLA Small architecture with the next-generation 208 and Corsa.

DS is targeting at least 310 miles of range, potentially reaching 342 miles, although battery capacities and power outputs remain unconfirmed. The N°3 would provide a stylish, more accessible entry point to DS ownership, complementing the relatively new N°4, N°7 and N°8 to complete a refreshed four-model family.


Peugeot has brought back one of its most distinctive names with the RCZ Vision, a striking electric coupé unveiled at the Paris Motor Show. Inspired by the original RCZ, the concept introduces Peugeot's new Feline Future design language, combining muscular proportions with sharp, futuristic detailing.

Beneath the dramatic bodywork lies equally ambitious technology, including a 500bhp electric powertrain, a solid-state battery and 1,000V architecture. Peugeot claims up to 372 miles of range and 10–80% charging in under ten minutes.

Although production remains unconfirmed, the RCZ Vision offers an exciting glimpse of how Peugeot could revive its sporting coupé heritage.


TNY Design Studio takes the RCZ Vision a step further, imagining how Peugeot's dramatic electric coupé could look as a production model. The original RCZ surprised many when Peugeot turned its striking concept into a showroom reality, proving that ambitious designs needn't remain motor-show fantasies.

From the RCZ to the elegant 508 and today's unconventional 408, Peugeot has a history of producing distinctive alternatives to conventional cars. A revived electric RCZ alongside the 408 could give the brand two aspirational non-SUV flagships.

Peugeot has arrived in Paris with an impressive collection of new concepts this year, suggesting its designers are feeling particularly adventurous.


Alongside the RCZ Vision, Peugeot has unveiled the extraordinary E-T16 Concept, a wild electric tribute to the legendary 205 Turbo 16 rally car. Developed with Peugeot Sport, the 816hp hyperhatch promises astonishing performance, accelerating from 0–186mph in just 16 seconds, while offering styling clues for the next-generation e-208.

Peugeot's third concept at Paris is the previously revealed Polygon, showcasing the brand's radical Hypersquare steering control and future design language.

Elsewhere, Peugeot is displaying its 9X8 endurance racing car and the iconic 205 GTi, alongside its complete production range. Together, they demonstrate Peugeot's renewed focus on distinctive design, technology and driving enjoyment.


Not everything Peugeot has brought to Paris is a futuristic concept. The French manufacturer is also showcasing its latest production model, the E-208 GTi, marking the long-awaited return of the legendary GTi badge.

Developed by Peugeot Sport, the electric hot hatch produces 281bhp and 345Nm of torque, reaching 62mph in just 5.5 seconds. Its 54kWh battery delivers up to 233 miles of WLTP range, while a lowered suspension, widened track and mechanical limited-slip differential promise genuine hot-hatch handling. UK prices start at £34,995.

And this isn't the end of Peugeot's Paris surprises, with the manufacturer promising another exclusive reveal on 18 October, the show's final day.


Vauxhall and Opel have unveiled the striking STX (Sports Tourer eXperimental) concept in Paris, offering a glimpse of the next generation of estate cars and the brand's evolving design language. Its sleek proportions, dramatic lighting and aerodynamic detailing introduce a more sophisticated interpretation of the familiar Vizor front end.

The STX also debuts Vauxhall's redesigned Griffin emblem, which loses its traditional flag for the first time.

Although not officially confirmed as the next Astra, the concept provides some intriguing clues about how a future Astra Sports Tourer could look, while introducing styling elements expected to influence Vauxhall's wider range from 2027.


Alfa Romeo has brought a particularly dramatic design statement to Paris with the Cuorerosso, a 4.7-metre, four-seat coupé intended to shape the brand's future rather than preview one specific production model. Its low silhouette, illuminated triangular grille and distinctive truncated rear reinterpret familiar Alfa Romeo styling, while rear-hinged doors add an unexpected touch of practicality.

Although the concept itself isn't destined for showrooms, Alfa Romeo says its design could influence future models across several segments. The manufacturer is also keeping its powertrain options open, from fully electric to hybrid, even imagining a 2.9-litre V6 full hybrid with Q4 all-wheel drive for future Quadrifoglio models.

It's an encouraging reminder that Alfa Romeo still considers distinctive styling and driving pleasure central to its identity.


Continuing through Stellantis's Italian brands, Fiat has brought something rather unusual to Paris with the Multiplay concept. Measuring 4.45 metres long, this versatile family vehicle can transform from a spacious six-seat MPV into a four-seat pickup, thanks to an ingenious sliding rear body section.

Inspired by Fiat's history of clever, affordable family transport, the Multiplay explores how one vehicle could serve several different purposes, combining everyday practicality with unconventional design.

Although production remains unconfirmed, the concept offers a fascinating glimpse of Fiat's future direction. It joins the existing Grande Panda and the newly introduced Grizzly and Grizzly Fastback at Paris, demonstrating the manufacturer's ambition to build a broader family of practical, affordable vehicles.


Fiat has also surprised Paris visitors with the much smaller Multiplina, a four-seat electric quadricycle inspired by the original 600 Multipla. Positioned between the tiny Topolino and conventional Fiat 500, it could offer an affordable, practical solution for urban families, with production reportedly being considered for 2028.

Just two years ago, Fiat's electric passenger-car range relied heavily on the 500e and 600e. Today, the Grande Panda, Grizzly family and expanding microcar line-up paint a very different picture, giving the Italian manufacturer an increasingly comprehensive range of small and medium-sized vehicles.

That concludes our look at Stellantis, whose remarkable collection of production launches, unexpected concepts and revived historic names has made it one of the dominant forces at this year's Paris Motor Show.


Moving on from Stellantis, we turn to Renault Group, another major presence at this year's Paris Motor Show. Between Renault, Dacia and Alpine, the French manufacturer has brought an impressive selection of new models, electric concepts and reinterpretations of familiar names.

Leading Renault's display is the striking E-Space Concept, a modern electric tribute to the original 1984 Espace. Measuring 4.7 metres long, it abandons today's SUV-inspired Espace styling in favour of a more traditional MPV silhouette, with enormous windows, six individual seats and a remarkably spacious, flexible interior.

Although Renault has no immediate plans to put it into production, the E-Space demonstrates that the company hasn't forgotten its pioneering approach to family transport.


TNY Design Studio explores how the E-Space could evolve into a production-ready seventh-generation Renault Espace, bringing the famous name back to its original purpose.

Rather than continuing down the SUV route, our interpretation imagines a more realistic electric MPV, preserving the concept's airy cabin, generous glass area and strong sense of space while adopting more conventional mirrors, lighting and body detailing.

Such a model would mark a clear return to the values that made the original Espace so influential: practicality, comfort and family-friendly versatility. In an SUV-dominated market, a revived Espace MPV could offer Renault a genuinely distinctive flagship once again.


Renault has brought its updated Mégane E-Tech Electric to Paris, featuring refreshed styling and improved technology. A new 67kWh LFP battery replaces the previous 60kWh unit, increasing WLTP range to 306 miles, while 15–80% charging takes just 24 minutes. Power remains at 220bhp, with UK prices starting at £28,245 after the full £3,750 Government Electric Car Grant.

The larger Scénic E-Tech has received similar attention, gaining an 89kWh battery offering up to 392 miles of WLTP range, with 15–80% charging in 28 minutes. A more affordable 67kWh LFP version is also planned for Europe, promising around 290 miles and faster charging.

With UK prices for the updated long-range Scénic starting at £33,245 after the Government grant, Renault's electric family-car range is looking increasingly competitive.


At the smaller end of Renault's electric range, the new Twingo E-Tech is making a big impression at Paris. The affordable city car combines an 80bhp motor with a 27.5kWh LFP battery, delivering up to 163 miles of WLTP range, while retaining the original Twingo's emphasis on clever interior packaging and everyday practicality.

The popular Renault 5 is also receiving important updates, including a new entry-level Five model with a 36.5kWh LFP battery, 110bhp motor and up to 190 miles of range. Existing 40kWh and 52kWh versions gain efficiency improvements too.

From the little Twingo through to the Mégane and Scénic, Renault's electric range is undergoing a substantial transformation, with improved technology, greater affordability and more choice across almost every segment.


Dacia is also using Paris to underline how rapidly its electric range is evolving. The new-generation Spring, now closely related to the just-revealed Renault Twingo E-Tech, promises a more mature and more competitive interpretation of the budget EV formula, while retaining the straightforward, affordable character that has made the model such a success.

Alongside it, Dacia is also previewing the larger Striker, broadening the brand's future line-up beyond the small cars. Together with its existing petrol, hybrid and bi-fuel models, the Spring and Striker show that Dacia is no longer approaching electrification cautiously. Instead, Paris makes clear that the brand is preparing a much wider and more confident next chapter.


At the other end of Renault Group's range, Alpine has unveiled the striking A310 Vision, a futuristic tribute to its distinctive 1970s sports coupé. Measuring 4.55 metres long and just 1.18 metres tall, the dramatic concept celebrates 55 years since the original four-cylinder A310 appeared, while exploring the design possibilities of Alpine's new Performance Platform.

Although not intended for production, it offers an intriguing glimpse of the brand's sporting future.

Elsewhere, Alpine is displaying a sculpture previewing the next-generation electric A110, alongside the A290 hot hatch in its new Collection specification. The larger A390 sports fastback also receives new personalisation options, colours and finishes, demonstrating Alpine's growing ambitions beyond traditional two-seat sports cars.


TNY Design Studio explores how Alpine's dramatic A310 Vision could evolve into a production-ready halo sports car, sitting above the upcoming electric A110. In this form, the A310 EV would bridge the gap between Alpine's lightweight, agile sports coupé and the larger, longer-range A390 fastback, giving the brand a more complete performance line-up.

Such a model could combine greater practicality and touring ability than the A110 with a more focused, emotional character than the A390. That would allow Alpine to offer something distinctive in the middle: a true grand touring sports coupé, designed to broaden the brand's appeal without losing its emphasis on style, performance and driver engagement.


Alpine isn't the only Renault Group brand bringing sporting excitement to Paris. Renault itself is displaying the striking 8 Gordini Concept, a modern electric tribute to its legendary 1960s performance saloon. Reimagined as a low, wide two-seat coupé, it combines rear-wheel drive and 270bhp with the original's unmistakable blue paintwork and twin white stripes.

Its minimalist, motorsport-inspired design shares a similar philosophy with the extraordinary Renault 5 Turbo 3E, also appearing at Paris with 555bhp and limited production planned from 2027. Unlike the Turbo 3E, however, the Gordini remains a one-off design exercise.

From affordable electric city cars to spacious family vehicles and ambitious performance concepts, Renault Group has delivered one of the show's most varied and interesting displays.


Volkswagen's biggest Paris attraction is the new ID. Tiguan, a substantial overhaul of the ID.4 that introduces a more familiar name. Featuring refreshed styling, an improved interior and up to 372 miles of WLTP range, it replaces both the ID.4 and coupé-styled ID.5 from early 2027, bringing the latter's production run to an end.

Elsewhere, Volkswagen is displaying the new ID. Polo GTI, producing 223 bhp featuring adaptive suspension, an electronically controlled limited-slip differential and sportier styling promise a more engaging driving experience.

Volkswagen is also showcasing the ID. Cross, updated ID.3 Neo and new 322bhp ID.3 GTI. Together, the displays highlight Volkswagen's increasingly broad electric range.


Audi has brought its new A2 e-tron to Paris, marking the return of a name last seen in 2005. Closely related to the Volkswagen ID.3 Neo, the compact electric hatchback starts at £30,700 after the £1,500 UK Government Electric Car Grant, giving Audi two hatchbacks around £30,000 alongside the petrol-powered A3.

The entry-level A2 produces 167bhp and offers 262 miles of WLTP range, while larger batteries extend this to an impressive 397 miles. Its aerodynamic design achieves a drag coefficient of just 0.24, with a practical 396-litre boot.

With the A1 and Q2 leaving production, the A2 represents an important new entry point into Audi ownership, prioritising efficiency, practicality and affordability over traditional premium-car dimensions.


Moving across Germany, Mercedes-Benz has brought another compact electric newcomer to Paris with the all-new GLA. Featuring an 85kWh battery, the GLA 250+ offers up to 406 miles of WLTP range, while its 800V electrical architecture enables charging at up to 320kW, adding approximately 168 miles in just ten minutes. A smaller 58kWh LFP version and a more powerful 4MATIC model broaden the range.

Mercedes is also showcasing the extraordinary electric AMG CLA 45, producing 671bhp from three electric motors. With all-wheel drive, 0–62mph takes just three seconds, while its 94kWh battery delivers up to 406 miles of range.

Together, they demonstrate how Mercedes is bringing impressive range, rapid charging and serious performance into its smaller electric models.


At the opposite end of Mercedes-Benz's electric range sits the extraordinary new AMG GT 4-Door Coupé, making its Paris show debut. Built around a dedicated electric performance platform, the flagship produces up to 1,153bhp, while the more restrained GT 53 offers 536bhp, a 106kWh battery and up to 503 miles of WLTP range. Charging at up to 600kW could add over 330 miles in just ten minutes.

Elsewhere, Mercedes is showcasing the electric VLE people carrier, new electric C-Class and GLC, alongside updated GLE and S-Class models.

Together with Audi and Volkswagen's launches, Mercedes rounds off an impressive German showing in Paris, demonstrating how the country's manufacturers are expanding their electric ranges from affordable hatchbacks to luxury flagships and extreme performance cars.


Bridging the gap between Germany and China, Smart has unveiled the new #2 at Paris, marking a welcome return to the tiny two-seat city cars that originally defined the brand. Now jointly owned by Mercedes-Benz and Geely, Smart has spent recent years expanding into larger electric SUVs, making the #2 something of a return to its roots.

Measuring just 2.75 metres long, the rear-wheel-drive newcomer produces 80bhp, with a 35.8kWh LFP battery promising up to 180 miles of WLTP range. Charging from 10–80% takes approximately 20 minutes.

Of course, this isn't Smart's first tiny electric two-seater. The original Fortwo Electric Drive arrived in 2007, eventually evolving into the EQ Fortwo, which remained in production until 2024.


Moving into China's increasingly ambitious Paris display, BYD has unveiled the Atto 8, its new seven-seat electric flagship. Measuring 5.04 metres long, the SUV introduces a 115kWh second-generation Blade Battery, delivering up to 405 miles of WLTP range in rear-wheel-drive form.

The extraordinary headline is FLASH Charging: BYD claims a 10–97% recharge in just nine minutes, using its dedicated ultra-rapid charging equipment.

The range-topping Excellence AWD produces 764bhp and reaches 62mph in 4.6 seconds, while still offering up to 374 miles of range. Inside, heated, ventilated and massaging seats across the first two rows underline its luxury ambitions, alongside a useful 136-litre front boot.

European sales begin in early 2027, although UK prices remain unconfirmed.


China's growing collection of electric superminis has gained another contender at Paris, where Chery is presenting the Q to European audiences for the first time. Despite its playful, rounded styling, it's a substantial 4.19 metres long, with a 2.70-metre wheelbase and a generous 375-litre boot, supplemented by a 70-litre front compartment.

A 119bhp electric motor is paired with a 41kWh battery, while 30–80% charging takes less than 17 minutes. Chery claims 249 miles of range, although this uses the older NEDC test rather than Europe's WLTP standard.

The Q demonstrates how Chinese manufacturers are increasingly challenging established European brands with affordable, practical electric hatchbacks. However, European pricing and UK availability remain unconfirmed.


Another small Chinese EV making its debut in Paris is the Aion UT Cross, a crossover-inspired version of the recently launched UT hatchback, itself a direct rival to the Chery Q we've just explored.

Developed at GAC's Milan design centre, the Cross sits 20mm higher than the standard UT, gaining rugged wheel arches, roof rails and wider tyres. Beneath the styling lies the same 60kWh LFP battery and 201bhp electric motor, while a generous 440-litre boot promises impressive practicality.

The regular UT offers 268 miles of WLTP range, although figures for the Cross remain unconfirmed. UK sales begin in early 2027, adding another affordable-looking contender to Europe's increasingly crowded small electric crossover market, with pricing still to be announced.


Continuing the growing selection of Chinese electric superminis, Leapmotor has brought its new B03 hatchback to Paris. Measuring 4.18 metres long, it's a direct rival to the Chery Q and promises impressive practicality, including a 405-litre boot and an additional 90-litre washable storage compartment.

A 53kWh LFP battery delivers up to 242 miles of WLTP range, while its 194bhp motor provides 0–62mph acceleration in 7.6 seconds. Rapid charging at up to 133kW allows a 10–80% recharge in just 21 minutes, with UK sales expected in early 2027.

Elsewhere, Leapmotor is showcasing its luxurious six- or seven-seat D19 flagship, alongside the B03X, B05, B10, C10 and T03. The company has also confirmed that European production of the B10 has begun in Spain, demonstrating its growing commitment to the European market.


Rounding off our look at China's growing presence in Paris, Omoda has brought its new entry-level 4 crossover to European audiences. Sitting beneath the Omoda 5, the sharply styled newcomer measures 4.42 metres long and offers a practical 402-litre boot.

Unlike the electric hatchbacks we've just explored, the Omoda 4 initially uses a 1.5-litre turbocharged full-hybrid powertrain, producing 221bhp and 295Nm of torque. A 1.83kWh battery supports the electric motor, while a fully electric version is also planned. UK sales are expected in 2027.

Together, the Chery Q, Aion UT Cross, Leapmotor B03 and Omoda 4 demonstrate the growing wave of smaller Chinese cars heading towards Europe. Yet Paris also showcases the other end of China's ambitions, with larger, increasingly luxurious models such as the BYD Atto 8, Leapmotor D19 and Zeekr 9X demonstrating how rapidly these manufacturers are expanding into premium territory.


South Korea's Hyundai has unveiled the second-generation Bayon at Paris, bringing a more substantial SUV design and improved practicality to its smallest crossover. Now measuring 4.25 metres long, it offers a generous 440-litre boot, alongside new technology including dual 12.3-inch displays. Initially available with 89bhp and 113bhp petrol engines, a 136bhp full hybrid will follow in 2027, broadening its appeal against increasingly competitive European rivals.

Elsewhere, Hyundai is showcasing the all-new Tucson and sportier N Line variant, alongside the electric Staria Cargo and recently introduced Ioniq 3 hatchback.

Sister brand Kia has brought the new Seltos Hybrid, featuring available electric all-wheel drive, alongside the K4 Hybrid hatchback and estate. Its expanding electric GT performance family and versatile PV5 passenger and commercial vehicles complete the display.

Together, Hyundai and Kia demonstrate an increasingly comprehensive range, combining affordable family transport, efficient hybrids and an expanding electric line-up.


Moving on to Japan, the country's manufacturers have a noticeably smaller presence in Paris this year. While Honda, Subaru and Toyota are attending, familiar names including Nissan, Mazda, Mitsubishi and Suzuki are absent.

Subaru is showcasing its new Uncharted electric SUV, a close relative of the Toyota C-HR+, sharing much of its underlying technology. Measuring 4.52 metres long, the Uncharted offers front-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive configurations, with up to 365 miles of WLTP range. The flagship dual-motor version produces 333bhp, reaching 62mph in approximately five seconds.

Paris also introduces the rally-inspired Uncharted ST-E edition, featuring gold alloy wheels and distinctive Impreza-inspired detailing. Alongside the larger electric E-Outback, it demonstrates Subaru's growing commitment to electric vehicles without abandoning its adventurous identity.


Subaru's second Paris exhibit is the E-Outback, an electric reinvention of its long-running raised estate. Closely related to the Toyota bZ4X Touring, it retains the Outback's adventurous character, combining a 633-litre boot, 211mm of ground clearance and a 1,500kg towing capacity.

Its dual electric motors produce 376bhp, delivering permanent all-wheel drive and 0–62mph acceleration in 4.5 seconds. A 74.7kWh battery provides up to 327 miles of WLTP range, with 10–80% charging taking approximately 28 minutes. Subaru's X-MODE off-road technology further distinguishes it from conventional electric family cars.

That concludes our look at Asia's contributions to Paris. Japan has maintained a relatively modest presence, while Hyundai and Kia demonstrate South Korea's increasingly comprehensive range of hybrids and electric vehicles. China, however, has arguably made the biggest impression, bringing an extraordinary variety of affordable electric hatchbacks, compact crossovers, luxurious SUVs and increasingly sophisticated technology. Europe's established manufacturers face competition from almost every direction.


The 2026 Paris Motor Show has demonstrated just how rapidly the automotive industry is evolving, with an impressive mixture of production-ready newcomers, ambitious concepts and familiar names making unexpected returns.

Stellantis and Renault Group have undoubtedly been among the show's biggest attractions, showcasing everything from affordable electric city cars to practical family vehicles and dramatic performance concepts. Their extensive displays also underline the importance of France's domestic manufacturers to one of Europe's most significant motoring events.

Yet the growing presence of Chinese manufacturers has been equally fascinating. With increasingly competitive small cars, sophisticated technology and ambitious luxury models, they're bringing fresh competition to nearly every corner of the European market.

For British buyers, the coming years promise greater choice, particularly as affordable electric cars finally begin receiving the attention they deserve.

With so many exciting developments still to come, Paris 2026 has provided plenty of reasons to look forward to the next generation of cars.

items.title: TNY Market Watch: Nine Family Car Bargains with Savings Up to £11,000
items.summary: Buying a practical family car doesn't have to mean spending £30,000 or more. While new-car prices have climbed considerably in recent years, pre-registered vehicles and discounted new-stock clearance offers continue to provide some remarkable bargains, often with thousands of pounds knocked off the original list price. From compact crossovers and spacious family…
items.content_html:
Chery Tiggo 4 1.5 Hybrid Aspire
Pre-reg price: £17,995
RRP: £19,995
Saving: £2,000

The Chery Tiggo 4 is already remarkably inexpensive at its full list price, making a further £2,000 reduction particularly appealing.

Unlike many affordable crossovers, it features a full-hybrid powertrain, combining a 1.5-litre petrol engine with electric assistance for a quoted 204PS system output. An automatic transmission comes as standard, while Aspire specification includes LED lighting, dual-zone climate control, a reversing camera and twin 12.3-inch displays.

Its compact SUV proportions provide useful family accommodation without making it awkward to park.

Chery remains a relatively new name in Britain, so long-term ownership and resale values are less established. Nevertheless, under £18,000 for a well-equipped full-hybrid automatic SUV represents impressive value.

Citroën C5 Aircross Hybrid 145 Plus
Pre-reg price: £23,998
RRP: £33,670
Saving: £9,672

The new-generation Citroën C5 Aircross is one of the largest and most comfort-focused cars in this selection, making its sub-£24,000 asking price especially interesting.

Its 145PS mild-hybrid petrol powertrain includes an automatic gearbox, while Citroën's Advanced Comfort suspension and supportive seating make it particularly appealing for longer family journeys.

A spacious rear cabin, generous luggage capacity and modern interior technology add to its appeal, with Plus specification offering an impressive level of equipment.

At almost £10,000 below list price, this pre-registered example brings a genuinely substantial, refined family SUV within reach of buyers shopping on a much smaller budget.

Dacia Bigster 1.2 Mild Hybrid Extreme
Pre-reg price: £23,495
RRP: £27,015
Saving: £3,520

Dacia's Bigster takes a more rugged, straightforward approach to family motoring, offering generous interior space and an enormous boot without the premium pricing often associated with larger SUVs.

The 1.2-litre turbocharged petrol engine produces 140PS with mild-hybrid assistance, balancing respectable performance with manageable running costs.

Extreme specification brings an adventurous appearance, 18-inch alloy wheels, modular roof bars and a panoramic opening sunroof, alongside a practical, hard-wearing interior designed for everyday family life.

At £23,495, the Bigster offers plenty of equipment, a substantial luggage compartment and the versatility of a large SUV for considerably less than many similarly sized alternatives. It's an appealing choice for families who prioritise space and everyday usability.

Hyundai Bayon 1.0 T-GDi Black Line
Pre-reg price: £17,000
RRP: £23,795
Saving: £6,795

The Hyundai Bayon combines compact dimensions with crossover styling and a surprisingly useful 411-litre boot, making it an interesting alternative to a conventional supermini.

The Black Line specification is particularly appealing, bringing distinctive dark exterior details, alloy wheels, heated front seats, a heated steering wheel, LED headlights and a 10.25-inch infotainment system.

Its 90PS turbocharged petrol engine is geared towards everyday economy rather than outright performance, but should prove perfectly adequate for commuting and family duties.

At £17,000, this pre-registered Bayon offers an attractive combination of equipment, practicality and manageable running costs.

MG S5 EV SE Standard Range
Pre-reg price: £17,995
RRP: £28,995
Saving: £11,000

Perhaps the biggest surprise here is the MG S5 EV. For less than £18,000, buyers can pick up a nearly new, fully electric family SUV with considerably more space than most similarly priced electric superminis.

The entry-level SE uses a 49kWh battery, offering approximately 211 miles of WLTP range, alongside rear-wheel drive and an automatic transmission. A 453-litre boot and spacious passenger compartment make it a genuinely useful family vehicle.

It won't match the longer-range versions for motorway flexibility, but the combination of modern technology, practical dimensions and an £11,000 saving against list price is difficult to ignore.

For households able to charge at home, this could be an exceptionally economical family car.

Nissan Juke 1.0 DIG-T N-Connecta
Pre-reg price: £15,999
RRP: £25,715
Saving: £9,716

At under £16,000, the Nissan Juke is the cheapest car in our selection, offering an affordable route into a nearly new family crossover.

The 1.0-litre turbocharged petrol engine produces 114bhp, while N-Connecta specification brings a 12.3-inch touchscreen, navigation, a 360-degree camera and 19-inch alloy wheels.

Its 422-litre boot makes it considerably more practical than its compact dimensions might suggest, although rear passenger space isn't as generous as some larger alternatives here.

The manual gearbox won't suit everyone, but with a discount of almost £10,000 against list price, this well-equipped Juke makes a compelling case for itself.

Peugeot 408 Hybrid Allure
Pre-reg price: £20,994
RRP: £32,065 
Saving: £11,071

Few cars in this selection offer quite as much visual presence as the Peugeot 408. Its distinctive fastback styling combines a low, sweeping roofline with raised suspension and a substantial 4.69-metre body.

Despite its unconventional appearance, the 408 offers genuine family practicality, including a generous 536-litre boot in the non-plug-in hybrid version.

The petrol-electric mild-hybrid powertrain includes an automatic gearbox, bringing useful efficiency improvements in town without requiring external charging. Allure trim adds a modern digital cockpit and a comfortable, well-equipped interior.

At barely £21,000, this represents a considerable amount of car for supermini money. The dramatic reduction against the list price makes it one of our most eye-catching finds.

Renault Symbioz 1.3 Mild Hybrid Techno
Pre-reg price: £20,894
RRP: £27,595
Saving: £6,701

Positioned between the Captur and Austral, the Renault Symbioz offers an appealing balance of manageable dimensions and genuine family practicality.

The 1.3-litre mild-hybrid petrol engine produces 140PS, providing stronger performance than many entry-level family crossovers, while official combined fuel economy approaches 48mpg.

A sliding rear bench allows owners to prioritise rear passenger space or luggage capacity, while Techno specification includes a 10.4-inch infotainment touchscreen with Google built-in, digital instruments and adaptive cruise control.

At just under £21,000, the Symbioz becomes a particularly interesting alternative to smaller SUVs, offering generous equipment and flexible accommodation.

Škoda Scala 1.0 TSI SE Edition
Pre-reg price: £16,900
RRP: £24,225
Saving: £7,325 

The Škoda Scala is one of the most overlooked family hatchbacks on sale. At 4.36 metres long, it's virtually identical in length to a Toyota Corolla hatchback, yet this pre-registered example costs less than many new superminis.

A substantial 467-litre boot, generous rear legroom and economical 1.0-litre turbocharged petrol engine make it an excellent everyday family car. SE Edition equipment includes LED headlights, a reversing camera, digital instruments and metallic paint.

Particularly appealing is the availability of both manual and seven-speed DSG automatic versions at £16,900. With no additional outlay for the automatic in these particular deals, the Scala offers remarkable practicality and equipment for the money.

— These nine cars demonstrate just how much value can be found by exploring pre-registered vehicles and discounted new-stock offers. From the affordable Nissan Juke and remarkably spacious Škoda Scala to the fully electric MG S5 and larger family SUVs, there's something here for almost every requirement.

With some models offering savings exceeding £10,000 against list price, buyers could find themselves driving a considerably larger, newer or better-equipped car than their budget might otherwise allow.

Stock and prices can change quickly, but for families prepared to shop around, pre-registration and clearance deals remain excellent ways to find genuine motoring bargains.

items.title: Škoda's Small Car Future: Cheaper EVs and a New Life for the Scala
items.summary: Škoda has built its reputation on delivering practical, spacious cars at sensible prices. Models like the Scala demonstrate just how much car the Czech manufacturer can offer for the money, but as the industry moves towards electrification, can Škoda bring that same value to its smallest electric models? The incoming Epiq is…
items.content_html:
Few cars demonstrate Škoda's approach to value quite as convincingly as the Scala. Starting at £24,225, it costs barely more than a Toyota Yaris at £23,995, yet at 4,362mm long, it's virtually identical in length to the considerably larger Toyota Corolla hatchback.

Its generous 467-litre boot is another highlight, offering the sort of luggage capacity that makes everyday family life considerably easier. Even the entry-level SE Edition includes LED headlights, a reversing camera, digital instruments and metallic paint, while economical petrol engines help keep running costs manageable.

The Scala might lack the Yaris's full-hybrid technology, but in terms of outright space and practicality for the money, it's an exceptionally appealing proposition.

This is what Škoda has traditionally done so well: delivering more car than buyers might expect for their money. The question now is whether it can bring that same philosophy to affordable electric motoring. (Image Credit: Škoda)

The new Škoda Epiq is a welcome addition, offering a generous 475-litre boot and approximately 190 miles of range from £24,950. But while it represents reasonable value for an electric SUV, there is surely room for something smaller and cheaper.

Fiat's distinctive Grande Panda Electric starts at around £21,500, while the stylish Renault 5 is available from £21,495 including the UK Government Electric Car Grant. Both demonstrate that affordable EVs can offer practicality and personality without breaking the bank.

Volkswagen's new ID. Polo starts at £23,945, sharing its MEB+ platform with the Epiq. Could Škoda use this engineering to develop a simpler, more affordable sister model?

TNY Design Studio imagines a Fabia EV, combining Škoda's latest Modern Solid styling with familiar supermini proportions and a target price of around £20,000.

Achieving that price would require careful cost-saving, but a practical, stylish electric Fabia could bring Škoda's traditional value philosophy to a new generation of buyers.
 Škoda is no stranger to affordable electric city cars. The original Citigoᵉ iV arrived in 2019, offering an 82bhp electric motor, a 36.8kWh battery and up to 160 miles of range. Despite measuring just 3.6 metres long, it offered four seats and a useful 250-litre boot.

Volkswagen is already preparing its next-generation electric city car, previewed by the ID. EVERY1 concept. Arriving in 2027, it targets a European starting price of around €20,000, potentially translating to approximately £18,000 in Britain.

Could Škoda take this affordable platform even further? TNY Design Studio imagines a reborn Citigo EV that could undercut its Volkswagen sibling, potentially becoming the Volkswagen Group's cheapest electric car.

Competition would be fierce. The new Renault Twingo is targeting a sub-£20,000 price, while the Leapmotor T03 and Dacia Spring already demonstrate just how affordable electric motoring can become.

A modern, practical Citigo EV could give Škoda a genuine entry-level electric car, positioned comfortably below the Fabia EV and Epiq.

Small electric crossovers are becoming an increasingly interesting part of the market, with models like the Hyundai Inster demonstrating how much practicality can be squeezed into a compact footprint.

TNY Design Studio imagines a Citigo Cross, combining the affordable engineering of our proposed Citigo EV with raised suspension, protective body cladding and more adventurous styling.

Sharing much of its engineering with the standard Citigo could help control costs, while a starting price under £20,000 would position it comfortably below the larger Epiq.

Could a tiny, affordable electric SUV help Škoda attract an entirely new group of buyers?

The Scala remains one of Škoda's strongest value propositions, so why abandon it? TNY Design Studio imagines a substantial Modern Solid facelift to keep the existing model looking fresh. Introducing Volkswagen Group's 1.0-litre TSI engine with 48V mild-hybrid technology, previously offered in the Golf, could also make plenty of sense.

From an affordable electric city car to a spacious family hatchback, Škoda has an opportunity to build on the qualities that have made it so appealing to value-conscious buyers. As electric cars become increasingly affordable, there's an opportunity to bring those same strengths to a new generation of smaller models.

The Epiq is a promising starting point, but a £20,000 Fabia EV, an even cheaper Citigo and a compact crossover alternative could help Škoda compete with the growing number of affordable electric rivals.

Meanwhile, keeping the Scala fresh and competitively priced would ensure that buyers seeking a practical, traditional family hatchback aren't forgotten.

These are possibilities rather than confirmed plans, but the opportunity is clear: Škoda doesn't need to reinvent its identity for the electric age. It simply needs to keep doing what it has always done best — offering genuinely good value.

items.title: What Are the Best Fun Cars You Can Buy for £6,000?
items.summary: A £6,000 budget opens the door to a surprisingly varied selection of interesting used cars. Rather than simply chasing the newest or lowest-mileage option, this is the point where buyers can start looking for something with real character. That might mean a proper rear-wheel-drive coupé, a lightweight hot hatch, a rare premium…
items.content_html:
BMW 428i 

The BMW 428i is one of the most powerful cars in this list, and our £6,000 budget should be enough to secure a 2014 example with around 100,000 miles.

Its 2.0-litre turbocharged petrol engine produces 242bhp, giving the 4 Series plenty of pace without turning it into an outright M-car. Better still, the 428i is rear-wheel drive, giving it a layout that is becoming increasingly rare among affordable coupés. It also feels like a proper step up from a hot hatch, with a low driving position, long bonnet and a much more grown-up cabin.

At this age, condition and service history matter more than mileage, but find a well-kept example and the 428i offers a lot of performance, style and proper coupé character for the money.


Ford Fiesta ST

The Ford Fiesta ST is one of the most obvious choices here, but that is because it remains one of the best small performance cars of its era.

Our £6,000 budget can secure a 2013 example with fewer than 60,000 miles, giving buyers plenty of choice without having to accept huge mileage. Its 1.6-litre turbocharged petrol engine produces 180bhp, sent to the front wheels through a six-speed manual gearbox.

The figures are respectable, but the real appeal is the chassis: quick steering, strong grip and a playful balance that makes the Fiesta feel entertaining even at sensible speeds. It is also practical enough to use every day, which helps explain why the ST has remained such an enduring favourite with enthusiasts.


Infiniti Q30 

The Infiniti Q30 is closely related to the Mercedes A-Class, but for the same sort of money it offers something rarer, more distinctive and arguably even more upmarket inside.

Our budget should secure a 2015 example with around 100,000 miles, putting this unusual premium hatch firmly within reach. Infiniti gave the cabin softer materials and a more heavily trimmed feel, helping the Q30 come across more like a small luxury car than a conventional premium hatchback.

The 2.2-litre diesel produces 168bhp and 350Nm of torque, giving it strong mid-range pull and making overtaking feel effortless. Add in the unusual styling, comfortable ride and scarcity on UK roads, and the Q30 makes a surprisingly compelling alternative to the far more common A-Class.


MINI Paceman Cooper S ALL4

The MINI Paceman Cooper S ALL4 is one of the strangest cars in this list, but that is also a big part of its appeal. Our £6,000 budget should secure a 2013 example with around 80,000 miles, putting this unusual MINI comfortably within reach.

Effectively a three-door coupé version of the Countryman, it mixes raised suspension, four-wheel drive and distinctive styling with a 1.6-litre turbocharged petrol engine producing 181bhp. The ALL4 system gives it useful extra traction in poor weather, while the compact proportions and MINI underpinnings help it retain plenty of character.

Inside, you get the oversized switches and circular detailing typical of MINIs from this era. It is quirky, quick and far rarer than the regular hatchback.


Peugeot 308 GTi

The Peugeot 308 GTi is one of the biggest performance bargains here. Our £6,000 budget should secure a 2016 example with fewer than 100,000 miles, and for that you get a serious hot hatch with huge power from just 1.6 litres.

In its most potent form, the turbocharged petrol engine produces 266bhp, and with relatively little weight to haul around, that translates into seriously strong performance. It is also more economical than the performance suggests, with around 40mpg achievable on a sensible run.

With diesel prices currently so high, that makes the GTi a surprisingly appealing everyday option as well as an entertaining one. Add sharp handling, understated styling and genuine pace, and the 308 GTi looks remarkably complete for the money.


Renault Twingo GT

France’s hot-hatch formula gets shrunk to city-car scale with the Renault Twingo GT. Its tiny 0.9-litre turbocharged three-cylinder engine produces 108bhp, mounted beneath the boot and driving the rear wheels.

Our £6,000 budget should put a 2016 example with around 60,000 miles within reach. Its appeal comes from the unusual rear-engined, rear-wheel-drive layout, light weight, playful character and relatively low running costs.

It is also surprisingly practical, with five doors, a tiny turning circle and enough room for city-car duties. Few modern small cars are configured anything like it, making the GT one of the most interesting choices here.


Saab 9-5

The second-generation Saab 9-5 is the unicorn of this list. Sold for only a brief period before Saab disappeared, it is now an exceptionally rare sight on UK roads, which makes simply finding the right one part of the experience.

Patient shoppers may even see the 2.8-litre turbocharged V6 appear close to our £6,000 budget, bringing serious performance to Saab’s final big saloon. More commonly, the diesels make a strong case of their own. The 2.0 TiD offers good economy and long-distance comfort, while the punchier twin-turbo TTiD adds much stronger performance without abandoning diesel efficiency.

Whichever version you find, the 9-5 combines distinctive styling, excellent safety credentials and genuine rarity in a way almost nothing else at this price can match.


Vauxhall Adam S

The Vauxhall Adam S is a small hot hatch with far more character than its badge might suggest. Our £6,000 budget should secure a 2015 example with fewer than 60,000 miles, making it one of the younger and lower-mileage cars in this list.

Its 1.4-litre turbocharged petrol engine produces 148bhp, which is plenty in something this compact, while the short wheelbase and firm setup give it an eager, playful feel around town and on a twisty road.

It also makes a great alternative to the more obvious Abarth 500, offering similar pint-sized performance with a little more space and a much rarer presence on UK roads. Add distinctive styling and reasonable everyday usability, and the Adam S is easy to like.

— £6,000 still buys an impressive amount of character if you are willing to look beyond the obvious choices. From lightweight hot hatches and rear-wheel-drive coupés to rare premium oddballs and one of Saab’s final cars, there is plenty here to make everyday motoring more interesting.

As ever at this end of the market, condition and history matter more than chasing the lowest mileage, but the right example can deliver far more personality than many much newer cars.
